name: Henana of Adiabene
knownFor: Master of the school of Nisibis, the school of the Church of the East in the Persian empire, in the late 500s, whose teaching is known only through his opponents. His opponents say he left the reading of Scripture taught by Theodore of Mopsuestia, and about three hundred students walked out in protest against him.
dates: Master of the school from 572 in Addai Scher's reckoning; J.-B. Chabot has him teaching there under the patriarch Ezekiel, about 570. Ignazio Guidi dates new school rules made while he was master to 590. No source used here gives his birth or death year
tradition: The Church of the East under Persia
role: Master of the school of Nisibis; interpreter of Scripture

keyWorks.title: Commentaries on Scripture
keyWorks.about: on Genesis, Job, the Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, the Twelve Prophets, Mark and the letters of Paul, with treatises on the faith, the sacraments and church feasts, as Abdisho of Nisibis lists them; none of them is held here

traces: Ignazio Guidi says new rules were added to the statutes of the school of Nisibis in 590, when Simeon was metropolitan of Nisibis and Henana was master of the school.
The Chronicle of Seert names Aha, Isaiah of Tahal and Meskena 'Arbaya as disciples of Henana who would not leave with Gregory's friends.
remembered: His pupil Barhadbeshabba calls him a man adorned with humility and with every gift that interpreting Scripture needs.
Mari ibn Sulayman says he had eight hundred students.
Babai the Great, his opponent, calls him Henana the heretic, the Chaldean and the follower of Origen.

uncertain: His teaching is known only through his opponents. Two witnesses agree that he left Theodore of Mopsuestia's reading of Scripture: the Chronicle of Seert, which writes against him, and Abdisho of Nisibis, who says many of his books were rejected because of Theodore. His pupil Barhadbeshabba says nothing of this; Addai Scher thinks the pupil probably hid the truth to praise his master.

The charges of fatalism and astrology, of following Origen and of denying the resurrection of the body rest on Babai the Great alone, in his Life of the martyr George. Oskar Braun calls Babai passionate and speaks of his exaggerations and contradictions. J. Labourt calls Babai Henana's antagonist; he cannot say whether the charge of fatalism is slander, though he finds it not implausible.

The synods. The synods that their editors date to 585, 596 and 605 defend Theodore's writings but never name Henana, as Braun notes. Chabot and Braun read a canon of the synod of 585 as aimed at him, and Labourt reads canons of 585 and 596 the same way. Braun adds that the defence of Theodore is aimed above all at the Monophysite party. Timothy I, a later head of the church, says the catholicos Sabrisho condemned Henana's writings.

His years. Scher reckons he became master in 572; Chabot says about 570. Scher's notes put his death under the catholicos Sabrisho, who died in 604, and elsewhere say he was still alive in 610. Babai, as Chabot reads him, writes of him as already dead.
The walk-out. The Chronicle of Seert says the students left with Gregory of Kashkar, metropolitan of Nisibis, and against Henana; Scher says Barhadbeshabba was among them.
